According to the manual, ecology is the study of...
Interactions between organisms and their surroundings
The classification and naming of living things
Weather patterns and climate over long periods
The structure of rocks, soils and landforms
Ecology is the study of interactions between organisms, their relationship to their surroundings and the processes taking place during these interactions.
Which of these does the manual list among the more important concepts in the study of ecology?
Adaptation, biodiversity and distribution of organisms
Anatomy, physiology and taxonomy of organisms
The manual names adaptation (behavioural and evolutionary), biodiversity and distribution of organisms as some of the more important concepts in ecology.
Why is it not enough to study each species or abiotic element on its own?
Biotic and abiotic parts of an ecosystem affect each other
Each species lives completely separately from others
Abiotic elements never change over time
Only large animals affect an ecosystem
Only by understanding how the biotic and abiotic components affect each other can we effectively conserve nature and biodiversity.
Which statement about ecosystems is correct?
They can be any size, from a fallen tree to the whole planet
They must be at least as large as a game reserve
They never exist inside larger ecosystems
An ecosystem can be of any size: a fallen tree, a river system, a game reserve, a biome, a continent or the entire planet. Small ecosystems exist within larger ones.
When does the manual say ecosystems are normally relatively stable?
When conditions are not substantially altered
Only when there are no predators present
When they contain a single species
Ecosystems are normally relatively stable provided the conditions are not substantially altered.
The wise use of renewable natural resources so that they benefit present AND future generations is called...
Conservation is the wise use of renewable natural resources for the greatest benefit of present generations while keeping their potential for future generations.
Hunting concessions where hunting is allowed but populations are carefully monitored are an example of...
The manual places hunting concessions under conservation because the sustainability of the animal populations is monitored.
A game reserve that does not allow any cutting of reeds or harvesting of fish is practising...
Preservation is the protection of all natural resources from any form of utilisation, allowing no external influences.
Which southern African mammal does the manual give as an example of an extinct species?
Extinction means not one living individual remains on Earth; the blue buck is the manual's example of an extinct southern African mammal.
In the biotic element of an ecosystem, the producers are...
The biotic element is divided into producers, which are autotrophs (green plants), consumers (heterotrophs) and decomposers (also heterotrophs).
Which of the following is part of the ABIOTIC element of an ecosystem?
The abiotic element is the non-living part of the environment: climate, soils and rocks, topography, altitude, latitude, water and nutrients.
All the pygmy geese living within a specific area form a...
A population is an intra-breeding group of the same species that shares a specific place and forms a single genetic unit, e.g. all the pygmy geese in an area.
All the populations of living organisms in an area
A single organism of one species
The non-living parts of an area
A group of the same species that breed together
A community is the combined population of all the living organisms in an area, from elephants down to algae.
The biotic community together with the abiotic component forms...
The manual states that the biotic community, together with the abiotic component, forms the ecosystem.
Produce their own food from abiotic substances
Feed only on dead plant and animal matter
Rely on other plants and animals for food
Collect food and store it for later
Autotrophs (producers) produce their own food; they are not dependent on other plants or animals but consume abiotic substances.
Using the meaning of '...vore', what does a piscivore eat?
'Vore' means to eat; piscivores eat fish, frugivores eat fruit and herbivores eat vegetation.
Which group of animals does the manual give as examples of browsers?
Browsers eat leaves, fruit, seeds and tips of branches; examples are kudu, eland and giraffe.
Which of these animals is given as an example of a grazer?
Grazers feed on grass; examples given are zebra, buffalo, tsessebe and wildebeest.
Animals such as squirrels that collect food and store it are called...
Foragers are animals that collect food and store it, such as squirrels.
Why are omnivores described as both primary and secondary consumers?
They eat both vegetation and animal flesh
They eat only dead and rotting material
They eat only insects and arthropods
They produce their own food from sunlight
Omnivores consume both vegetation and the flesh of animals, so they are both primary and secondary consumers.
Which animal does the manual list as an omnivore?
Omnivores listed include humans, baboons, warthog and jackal.
Shrews, pangolins, aardvarks and bat-eared foxes are examples of...
Insectivores are secondary consumers that eat almost only insects and other arthropods, e.g. shrews, pangolins, aardvarks, bat-eared foxes and aardwolf.
Termites, dung beetles, fungi and many bacteria are classified as...
Detritivores/decomposers feed only on dead and/or decomposing plant and animal matter; examples include termites, dung beetles, carrion beetles, fungi and bacteria.
Why are lions and leopards NOT classified as true scavengers?
Scavenging is not their main source of food
They never feed on dead animals
Lions and leopards are known to scavenge, but this is not their principal source of food, so they are not true scavengers.
Two impala rams fighting for dominance during the rut is an example of...
Intra-specific competition ('intra' means within) is competition between individuals of the same species for a resource in short supply.
A woodland kingfisher and a Meves's starling competing for nesting holes is an example of...
Inter-specific competition ('inter' means between different) is competition between two different species for the same scarce resource.
The actual area where a species population does exist
The conditions in which a species could possibly live
The area shared by species competing for food
The place where a species breeds only
A realised niche is the actual area in which a species population does exist.
Why is the fundamental niche usually larger than the realised niche?
It does not consider competition from other species
It only includes the breeding area
It ignores the need for food and water
It is measured only during the wet season
The fundamental niche is hypothetical and does not consider competition from other species, so it is usually larger than the realised niche.
An area that is common to more than one species competing for the same food is called...
An overlap niche is the area common to more than one species competing for the same food.
The parasite benefits and the host is harmed
One benefits and the other is unaffected
Parasitism is a symbiotic relationship where the parasite benefits but the host is harmed.
How does parasitism differ from predation?
Parasites are usually smaller and do not always kill the host
Parasites are always larger than their hosts
Parasites always kill the host quickly
Parasites only feed on dead animals
The parasite is usually smaller than its host, and while predators kill their prey, parasites do not necessarily kill the host.
According to the manual, what does the sour plum do as a partial parasite?
Its roots take nutrients from the roots of nearby grasses
It grows high in the canopy of acacia trees
It traps small insects in bladders on its roots
It feeds on sugars in the bark of mopane trees
The sour plum is a partial parasite sending its roots to remove nutrients from the roots of nearby grasses.
Oxpeckers feeding on ticks found on a giraffe is an example of...
Mutualism is a relationship where both partners benefit: the oxpeckers get food and the giraffe is rid of parasites.
How does the marula tree benefit when an elephant eats its fruit?
Its seed is spread in a nitrogen-rich heap of dung
The elephant prunes its lower branches
The elephant protects it from other browsers
The elephant gets nutrition, while the tree's seed is spread in a nitrogen-enriched heap of manure, so both benefit (mutualism).
Cattle egrets catching grasshoppers disturbed by moving buffalo is an example of...
In commensalism one partner benefits (the egret) while the other (the buffalo) is unaffected.
Why do blue waxbills often build their nests next to paper-wasp nests?
The wasps protect them from predators
The wasps keep the nest cool
The waxbills feed on the wasp larvae
The waxbills are protected from predators by the wasps, while the wasps are not rewarded in any way (commensalism).
A habitat type is normally named after...
The type of rock underneath it
Habitat types are normally named after the dominant vegetation, e.g. acacia woodlands, floodplains and grasslands.
The thin layer above and below the Earth's surface that sustains all life is the...
The biosphere is the thin layer above and below the Earth's surface that sustains all life, including biotic and abiotic parts.
The country they are found in
Biomes are mainly defined by vegetation; e.g. the savannah biome is defined by its mix of grassland and woodland.
How many biomes are recognised in southern Africa?
There are nine recognised biomes in southern Africa, including savannah, grassland, forest and fynbos.
Which is the largest biome in southern Africa?
The savannah biome is the largest biome in southern Africa.
What is the annual rainfall range of the savannah biome?
The structure of the savannah depends on rainfall, which ranges from 200mm to 1000mm per annum.
How does the savannah tree canopy differ from that of the forest biome?
In savannah the canopy almost never touches
In savannah the canopy is always closed
Savannah has no trees at all
In the savannah the tree canopy almost never touches, as it does in the forest biome.
Why does the savannah biome have a high carrying capacity?
Leaves at many browsing levels plus abundant grazing
It has very little competition between species
It receives over 2000mm of rain a year
Leaves of trees and shrubs at various browsing levels, plus abundant grazing, give the savannah a high carrying capacity and broad species diversity.
In the energy flow described in the manual, which level eats the carcasses of dead carnivores?
When the carnivores die, the scavengers (tertiary consumers) eat the carcasses.
Herbivores use about 90% of the energy from plants. How much is left for carnivores?
Herbivores use 90% of the energy for respiration, digestion, movement etc., leaving only 10% for the carnivores.
What percentage of the original plant energy reaches the scavengers (tertiary level)?
After herbivores and carnivores each use 90%, only 1% of the original plant energy is available to the scavengers.
Which organisms are described as the essential link in the nutrient cycle?
Decomposition of dead organisms makes nutrients available to other life forms; decomposers are the essential link in this cycle.
According to the manual, the food chain starts with...
Sunlight transformed into energy by plants
The food chain starts with sunlight, which is transformed into energy by plants.
Many food chains all interacting with one another
A single chain from plant to predator
The energy lost as metabolic heat
The abiotic base of the trophic pyramid
The food web is the interwoven link between many producers and consumers and may be viewed as a number of food chains interacting.
